known_python_bugs.what: self._species[match] and the reported 'key' both use `match`, a *lowercased scientific name*, as if it were a DB key. True for the training DB (keys are scientific_name.lower()) but not for data/app/augury-ondevice.json, where 5 species differ: cenchrus spp / Cenchrus spp., rytidosperma spp / Rytidosperma spp. (formerly Austrodanthonia), sporobolus spp / Sporobolus spp., swainsona spp / Swainsona spp., wahlenbergia spp / Wahlenbergia spp. On the app DB this raises KeyError and aborts the entire search.
known_python_bugs.fixture_workaround: install_search_bug_workaround(): _species.__getitem__ resolves a lowercased scientific name to its key, and safe_search() remaps a fabricated result key back to the real key (dropping the entry if there is none). The Kotlin port indexes scientific names explicitly and never fabricates a key.

known_python_bugs.what: merged_indicators() returns `sources` (which sibling supplied the rows) but _result() never uses it; the parameter is dead.
known_python_bugs.fixture_workaround: none needed - the Kotlin port does not expose it

known_python_bugs.what: bad_values is re-built as a set from an already-sorted list, and str hashing is randomised per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the order in which values are excised is not deterministic. The order matters when one value is a substring of another (e.g. '6' vs '6.5'). The Kotlin port iterates the sorted unsupported-values list, which is the order verify() reports.

known_python_bugs.where: SpeciesDB._sanitize() vs the shipped app database
known_python_bugs.what: Not a bug in Python, but an inconsistency worth recording: _sanitize() deletes junk keys from _species entirely, while data/app/augury-ondevice.json keeps them and tags them specificity='junk'. The Kotlin port follows the app DB (keeps them, filters at match time via _best_plant_match) because junk_keys.py documents that a user pasting e.g. 'dandelion clay' should still get an honest answer.

indicators.Soil pH: Weeds Australia states serrated tussock 'will grow in acid soils', so its presence is compatible with acidic soils; no alkaline limit is given. NSW WeedWise gives no pH figure and no Australian source consulted stated a numeric pH range.
indicators.Moisture: Occupies both dry and moist ground - Weeds Australia places it 'on low-fertility and dry soils' as well as on 'fertile moist flats' - and it is drought tolerant, with drought-caused bare ground favouring it. Its distribution is 'limited by salinity and / or water-logging', so its presence indicates ground that is not waterlogged.
indicators.Fertility: Indicates low soil fertility / nutrient-poor soil. NSW WeedWise states 'Sandy, nutrient poor soils are at most risk' of invasion, and Weeds Australia lists 'low-fertility and dry soils' among the situations it grows on (while noting it also grows on 'rich to poor degraded soils').
indicators.Salinity: Indicates non-saline soil. NSW WeedWise lists 'saline soils or salty areas' among the situations serrated tussock 'does not grow well in', and Weeds Australia states its distribution 'is limited by salinity'.
indicators.Soil type: Tolerates 'shallow soil if it is not in competition with other plants' and grows on 'soils derived from basalt, granite, shale, slate and sandstone' (NSW WeedWise). Weeds Australia describes it as 'adapted to a wide range of climates and soil types', growing 'from steep, rocky and timbered areas, on low-fertility and dry soils, to fertile moist flats'. No single texture preference is stated by either source.
indicators.Disturbance: A strong bare-ground/disturbance indicator. NSW WeedWise: 'Serrated tussock colonises bare areas. Drought causing bare ground favours serrated tussock.' Weeds Australia: it 'quickly colonises bare ground and disturbed areas such as roadsides, overgrazed pastures or cultivated situations', and its seedlings are 'usually out-competed by other plants, but become competitive under conditions of drought or overstocking when more favourable pasture species are consumed by stock'.
indicators.General indicators: Temperate south-eastern Australia (far north-eastern NSW south to Victoria and eastern Tasmania), on pastures, native grasslands, open scrub and woodland, roadsides, overgrazed pastures and cultivated situations; cool temperate areas with 450-1000 mm annual rainfall, on all terrain and aspects, from steep rocky timbered country to fertile moist flats; also invades urban roadsides, railways, power-line easements and reserves.

indicators.Soil type: NSW DPIRD: 'Plants prefer light soil with high soil moisture in spring and summer', and it has been 'found growing in ... native pastures with sandy soils'. Landscape SA (Kangaroo Island): 'prefers light soil'. Weeds Australia: grows 'mainly on light soils'. HerbiGuide: 'Light soils or loams mainly.'
indicators.Moisture: Landscape SA: 'a summer growing perennial plant that prefers light soil, warm conditions and high soil moisture over spring and summer. It grows rapidly in irrigated pastures and crops.' NSW DPIRD: 'Plants prefer light soil with high soil moisture in spring and summer.' Indicates summer-moist / irrigated ground, not dryland.
indicators.Disturbance: Landscape SA: 'Infestations mostly occur where vehicles traverse and stock compound soil' (i.e. bare, compacted, stock-camped ground). NSW DPIRD lists 'stock routes and sale yards' and 'disturbed areas such as roadsides'. Weeds Australia: khaki weed 'does particularly well colonising bare or disturbed areas'.
indicators.General indicators: Tropical, subtropical, semi-arid and warm temperate climates of NSW (all regions of NSW and all Australian states). Recorded in stock routes and sale yards, native pastures with sandy soils, grasslands, orchards, disturbed areas such as roadsides, urban gardens/lawns/parks/recreation areas, caravan parks and camping grounds (NSW DPIRD). Also irrigated pastures and crops, and around towns on nature strips, playing fields and saleyards (Landscape SA; Weeds Australia).

indicators.Soil type: AWRI's soil-indicator entry states caltrop 'occurs on a wide range of soils but is more abundant on sandy soils'. Weeds Australia (quoting Parsons & Cuthbertson 1992) places it 'mostly in open waste places ... particularly in districts with high summer temperatures and dry sandy soils where there is little competition'. HerbiGuide: 'Occurs on a wide range of soils. More abundant on sandy soils.'
indicators.Moisture: AWRI: caltrop 'is drought tolerant but is intolerant to waterlogging'. The Victorian Weed Risk Assessment (VRO, archived) records 'its extensive root system allows it to survive droughts' and that 'seeds germinate after late spring and summer rains'. Net reading: dry, well-drained, summer-moist sites; not waterlogged ground.
indicators.Fertility: AWRI lists caltrop as 'an indicator of low calcium, very low potassium and organic matter, high phosphorus, magnesium, iron, and aluminium' - i.e. an indicator of nutrient imbalance rather than of generally high fertility. The page gives no primary citation for this indicator list (its linked resource is HerbiGuide), so treat as medium confidence.
indicators.Organic matter: AWRI lists caltrop as an indicator of 'very low ... organic matter' in the soil.
indicators.Disturbance: SA PIRSA: 'Caltrop is favoured by bare ground, and does not compete effectively with other plants. Management to maintain a dense ground cover significantly reduces germination.' AWRI quotes a Henschke Wines case study: caltrop 'hates competition', found isolated to 'bare patches of soil on headlands' and spread on vehicle tyres.
indicators.General indicators: Open waste places, roadsides, overgrazed pastures, stock yards and neglected areas; also crops and orchards/vineyards; districts with high summer temperatures and little competition (Weeds Australia, quoting Parsons & Cuthbertson 1992). PIRSA lists habitat simply as 'gardens, pastures'. HerbiGuide lists 'pastures, crops, vineyards, orchards, cotton, horticulture, roadsides, stockyards, bushland, parks, stock routes and disturbed areas'.
